Defender of Halakha and Watchman in the Time of Confusion: The Work, Torah Teaching and Polemical Teaching of Hakham Yaakov Sasportas
This text surveys the life and teaching of Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas, an influential rabbinic figure who was active in the 17th century and became known mainly as the leading fighter against Sabbateanism. The article traces the course of his turbulent life between North Africa and Europe, emphasizing his uncompromising halakhic authority and his illustrious family descent from Nahmanides. Alongside an analysis of his Torah works, such as the responsa "Ohel Yaakov," it details his complex attitude to Kabbalah and his firm opposition to any deviation from communal custom. Finally, the source focuses on his polemical work "Tzitzat Novel Tzvi," which serves as historical testimony to his lonely struggle against the false messiah Shabbetai Tzvi, and assesses his intellectual legacy as a gatekeeper who set the rationality of halakha against messianic ecstasy.
Defender of Halakha and Watchman in the Time of Confusion: The Work, Torah Teaching and Polemical Teaching of Hakham Yaakov Sasportas
Stations of Life and Upheavals of Fate: A Political and Spiritual Biography
Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas (1610–1698) was active in one of the most turbulent and dramatic periods in the history of the Jewish people in the early modern era [cite: 1, 2, 3]. He was born in Oran in Algeria to Rabbi Aharon, the son of a distinguished family of exiles from Spain that proudly traced its lineage back to Nahmanides, from whom Sasportas was considered to be of the eleventh generation [cite: 1, 4]. This precious lineage was not merely a source of personal family pride but served as an essential means of establishing his Torah authority in the eyes of his students and listeners [cite: 4]. One of the most prominent of his students, Rabbi Yechiel Mehatov, expressed this awareness in his letters, signing with reverence and noting his renowned teacher's standing in the received tradition of his fathers, in the sixty gates distinguished in halakha, of the seed of Nahmanides [cite: 4]. Already in his childhood the boy Yaakov stood out for his extraordinary talents, and already at the age of nine he amazed his teachers with his broad knowledge of the Talmud and the halakhic decisors [cite: 4].
At the age of only eighteen he was appointed a member of the rabbinic court in the city of Tlemcen, and at the age of twenty-four he was chosen to serve as head of the rabbinic court and halakhic authority in that city and in other communities in North Africa [cite: 1, 4]. Already in his youth, even before the wrath of the authorities in Tlemcen struck him, Sasportas's decisive halakhic influence was evident beyond the bounds of his local community [cite: 4, 5]. Clear historical testimony to this is found in a long halakhic responsum that he sent in 5402 (1642) from the city of Salé to Fez [cite: 5]. This early responsum, a copy of whose manuscript survived and was later printed with slight textual variations in the responsa "Ohel Yaakov" (section 8), shows that already at the age of thirty-two Sasportas was regarded as a halakhic decisor of stature whose door the diasporas of North Africa sought out [cite: 4, 5]. In 5407 (1647) a dramatic turning point occurred in his life when he became embroiled in a serious conflict with the ruler of Tlemcen [cite: 4]. He was imprisoned, cruelly tortured in chains, and all his money was taken from him on false charges [cite: 4, 6]. After his release he was forced to flee to Salé in Morocco, where he found temporary refuge, living in constant fear of the authorities, and in this period he married Mrs. Rachel, the daughter of Hakham Daniel Toledano, who was the rabbi of Meknes [cite: 3, 4].
In 5411 (1651) Sasportas decided to emigrate to Europe and settled in liberal Amsterdam [cite: 1, 4]. There he printed his first work, "Toldot Yaakov" [cite: 3, 7]. In 5416 (1656) he was among the members of the diplomatic delegation organized by Hakham Menasseh ben Israel to the Lord Protector Oliver Cromwell in London, with the aim of requesting permission for the return of the Jews to England [cite: 1, 3]. Three years later, in 5419 (1659), he returned to North Africa and was sent on an official diplomatic mission on behalf of the king of Morocco to the king of Spain [cite: 1, 4]. After another brief stay in Salé, from which he was forced to flee because of the political instability, famine and drought that struck Morocco, he returned to Amsterdam, and in 5424 (1664) he was appointed rabbi of the Sephardic community in London [cite: 1, 4]. Two years later, in the midst of the Great Plague of 1666, which killed tens of thousands, he was forced to leave London and moved to Hamburg in Germany [cite: 1, 4]. In Hamburg his standing as the chief fighter against Sabbateanism grew stronger [cite: 1]. After the messianic storm had subsided, he was invited in 5433 (1673) by the wealthy brothers of the Pinto family to return to Amsterdam, where he headed the "Keter Torah" study hall [cite: 3, 4]. In 5435 (1675) he moved to Livorno in Italy, where he served as a rabbinic judge and head of a yeshiva, but in 5440 (1680) he quarreled with the community and its rabbis and left the city [cite: 1, 3, 4].
His public authority and the legitimacy of his rulings found clear expression also beyond the narrow bounds of the Portuguese community in Amsterdam. Thus, for example, in 5440 (1680), Rabbi Sasportas was called to act in The Hague at the request of the lady Mrs. Rachel Suasso de Pinto, in order to obtain from the local Dutch authorities the legal permits needed to set up an eruv in the city [cite: 3]. This request points to his unique diplomatic and Torah standing, which enabled him to bridge between the stringent demands of halakha and the civil authorities in liberal Europe [cite: 1, 3]. In 5444 (1684) he returned to Amsterdam for good and headed the "Etz Chaim" yeshiva, and in 5453 (1693), upon the death of Hakham Isaac Aboab da Fonseca, he was appointed to take his place as chief rabbi of the Sephardic community in Amsterdam [cite: 1, 3]. He held this high office until the day of his death on 4 Iyar 5458 (1698), and was buried in the magnificent Portuguese cemetery "Beth Haim" in Ouderkerk [cite: 1, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Method of Ruling and Halakhic Authority in the Responsa "Ohel Yaakov"
Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas's halakhic teaching is characterized by an uncompromising striving to establish the authority of pure halakha, relying on sound reasoning, rational analysis and a resolute struggle against changes in custom not anchored in the accepted tradition of ruling [cite: 12, 13, 14]. His rulings, collected in the book of responsa "Ohel Yaakov," reflect a theological position that sees halakha as the sole protective wall of the Jewish community against spiritual and social anarchy [cite: 2, 13, 15]. Sasportas held a lofty self-conception of his Torah authority, as he wrote in his famous letter to Rabbi Saul Morteira, in which he stressed that his way was to correspond with the great rabbis of the diaspora who sought his opinion, and that his words and rulings were not said for the sake of his personal honor but for the honor of God's Torah and the revelation of absolute truth [cite: 1].
Further testimony to Sasportas's extensive legal activity in Europe is his halakhic cooperation with the great sages of his generation, among them the physician-sage Rabbi Benjamin Mussafia [cite: 11]. In 5432 (1672) the two were called upon to decide jointly one of the complex questions in the laws of monetary matters and inheritance, which concerned the estate of a widow who had passed away [cite: 11]. This ruling, published under the title "Edut be-Yaakov," reflects not only the depth of Sasportas's financial rulings but also his central standing in shaping Jewish law in the Sephardic communities of northern Europe [cite: 11].
An in-depth analysis of his rulings reveals a number of fundamental principles in his method of ruling:
A. Denying Coercive Authority to One Not of Pedigree within the Congregation of Israel
In his famous responsum in "Ohel Yaakov" (section 4), Sasportas discusses the question of appointing a righteous convert to public offices of an authoritative character [cite: 16]. He utterly rejected the possibility of appointing a convert to the post of parnas (community leader) or charity warden, relying on the halakhic principle according to which offices involving dominion and coercive authority must be given only to one who is "from among your brothers" [cite: 16]. Sasportas distinguished between these posts and the post of treasurer: whereas the parnas and the warden are empowered to coerce the public and to take pledges of property for the purposes of taxes and charity (and therefore appointing a convert to these posts is forbidden), the treasurer deals only in technical financial management without coercive authority, and therefore a convert may be appointed to it [cite: 16]. This distinction shows his acute sensitivity to the class structure of the community and to preserving the boundaries of legitimate authority [cite: 16].
B. Firm Opposition to Liturgical Innovation as an Expression of Sabbateanism
During the days of Sabbatean confusion, the believers in Shabbetai Tzvi in Amsterdam introduced an unusual custom of the Priestly Blessing (the raising of the hands) every Sabbath, contrary to the tradition of the community according to which they blessed only on festivals [cite: 8, 17]. In the responsa "Ohel Yaakov" (sections 68–69, 71) Sasportas launched a sharp attack against this custom [cite: 17]. He determined that this was not an addition of holiness but a serious breach threatening to topple the stability of custom, and defined the blessing as a curse coming from the influence of "Balaam the wicked" (a hint by gematria to Shabbetai) and the instructions of the false prophet "the child Zedekiah son of Chenaanah" (a hint by gematria to Nathan of Gaza) [cite: 8]. This ruling illustrates how Sasportas identified in every slight change of custom an existential danger to the rule of halakha [cite: 8, 12].
The scholarly preparation and editing of the book of responsa "Ohel Yaakov," which was published only after the author's death in 5497 (1737), likewise reflect the importance that the next generation attributed to his teaching [cite: 3, 17]. The book was prepared for print and carefully proofread by the renowned proofreader Rabbi David Meldola, who labored over the arrangement of the abridgment and its sources and added at its end a detailed and precise index [cite: 8, 17]. Meldola, who was at that time responsible for proofreading other central works such as the responsa of the Tashbetz and the book "Mayim Rabbim" by his father, Rabbi Raphael Meldola, gave "Ohel Yaakov" its final scholarly form [cite: 8]. The work won enormous esteem and was accompanied by the approbations of the great sages of the generation, headed by the holy gaon Rabbi Elazar of Krakow, head of the rabbinic court of the Ashkenazi community in Amsterdam and author of the well-known work "Ma'aseh Rokeach" on the Mishnah [cite: 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Kabbalistic Teaching and His Attitude to the Esoteric Torah
A deep and essential insight for understanding the figure of Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas concerns his complex and ambivalent attitude to the teaching of Kabbalah. Contrary to a mistaken historiographical conception that tries to portray Sasportas as a dry rationalist opposed to the world of mysticism, the historical sources prove that he himself was a distinguished kabbalist who greatly valued the esoteric teaching [cite: 6, 12]. His attitude to Kabbalah is based on a sharp distinction between traditional, institutionalized Kabbalah, fully subject to the authority of halakha, and anarchic Sabbatean Kabbalah, which seeks to break through the boundaries of the practical commandments [cite: 12, 13].
In 5413 (1653), during his first stay in Amsterdam, Sasportas brought to print the book "Heichal ha-Kodesh" by the 16th-century Moroccan kabbalist Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon Elbaz [cite: 6, 9, 10]. This work, which explains the order of the prayers and their intentions according to the way of Kabbalah, is considered one of the important works to emerge from the teaching of the kabbalists of the Maghreb in that period [cite: 9, 10]. Sasportas edited the book, wrote for it a long scholarly introduction called "Penei Heichal," and thereby established his standing as a spiritual authority well versed in the mysteries of Kabbalah [cite: 6, 10].
Elbaz's work was accompanied by valuable glosses and explanations based on the teaching of the Ari, of blessed memory, written by the Moroccan kabbalist Rabbi Aharon ha-Siboni [cite: 9, 10]. Sasportas saw this combination of North African Kabbalah with the studies of the kabbalists of Safed as a vital means of deepening the religious and liturgical experience of the individual, as long as it remains anchored within the bounds of institutionalized prayer and the commandments of the Torah [cite: 9, 10]. This distinction later guided him in his war against Sabbateanism: he did not attack the very use of the Zohar or of kabbalistic concepts, but the fact that the Sabbateans (such as Nathan of Gaza or Abraham Michael Cardozo) used these holy writings to justify grave transgressions, the cancellation of fast days and the permitting of clear halakhic prohibitions [cite: 2, 18, 19]. In Sasportas's eyes, true Kabbalah is Kabbalah that gives expression to the virtues of the commandments and the yoke of halakha, whereas Kabbalah cut off from religious practice is a strange and dangerous fire [cite: 12, 20].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The War to the Bitter End against Sabbateanism and the Creation of Tzitzat Novel Tzvi
In the years 1665–1666 an unprecedented wave of messianic ecstasy swept the Jewish world [cite: 2, 15]. The appearance of Shabbetai Tzvi as messiah and the prophesying of Nathan of Gaza carried along whole communities, including spiritual leaders, rabbinic judges and community leaders, who publicly declared their belief in the imminent redemption [cite: 12, 21]. Many Jews, seized by religious enthusiasm, sold all their property and waited for the longed-for sign to go up to the Land of Israel [cite: 12].
Rabbi Sasportas, who was then staying in Hamburg, stood almost alone at the forefront of the struggle against the general messianic madness [cite: 1, 15, 22]. He sent dozens of sharp epistles and letters to the communities of Israel throughout the world, in which he denounced Shabbetai Tzvi as an impostor and warned the masses not to be caught in his net [cite: 1, 4, 6].
The Formation of the Work and the Mutual Relations with the Opponents in the Field
During the months of the struggle, Sasportas meticulously collected all the epistles, documents and correspondence he conducted with supporters and opponents of the movement, and bound them into a trenchant work in four parts called "Tzitzat Novel Tzvi" [cite: 1, 18]. The title of the book alludes cynically to the verse in Isaiah: "And the fading flower of his glorious beauty shall be..." [cite: 18].
In his uncompromising struggle, Sasportas found few but determined allies among the spiritual leadership of the period. The most prominent of them was his colleague Hakham Rabbi Yosef Buino (the Ri Buino), who stood with him on a single front against the messianic sect [cite: 23]. The scholarly mutual relations between the two grew ever deeper; the Ri Buino compiled a comprehensive collection on the customs of Jerusalem, a work that won such great esteem that the author of the "Peri Chadash" later copied it in full [cite: 23]. The joint stand of Sasportas and Buino against the waves of messianic enthusiasm provided the scholarly anchor that the communities needed in order to identify the deviation from the accepted tradition [cite: 23].
The Controversy over Censorship and the Ban on the Book
Sasportas's great book was not printed in his lifetime [cite: 1]. The history of the book in print is accompanied by public storm and sharp communal censorship:
The decree of the ban in Amsterdam: when the book of responsa "Ohel Yaakov" was printed in 1737, it included at its end the appendix "Kitzur Tzitzat Novel Tzvi" (the abridgment of Tzitzat Novel Tzvi) prepared by Rabbi David Meldola [cite: 1, 8, 17]. The leaders of the Portuguese community of Amsterdam (the "Ma'amad") saw in the publication of the old epistles, which showed that their fathers had followed the false messiah, a grave affront to the honor of the families [cite: 8, 17]. They decreed a severe ban and ordered that all the pages containing the abridgment be removed from the books of responsa and handed over for genizah [cite: 8, 17]. Because of this decree, almost all the copies of the first edition were destroyed and disappeared from the market [cite: 8, 17].
The rescue of the work by the Yaavetz: only in 1757 (5517) was the abridgment reprinted in Altona at the printing house of Rabbi Yaakov Emden (the Yaavetz) [cite: 24, 25]. The Yaavetz, who discovered a rare copy that had survived the burning, defined it as "a brand plucked from the fire" and redistributed it in order to continue his struggle against the remnants of Sabbateanism in his generation [cite: 8, 24].
The discovery of the complete edition: the full book, in its four parts, did not see print until 5714 (1954), when the scholar Isaiah Tishby published a complete scholarly edition with the Bialik Institute, based on the complete "Epstein manuscript" found in the estate of Zechariah Schwarz [cite: 1, 18].
The Rewriting Controversy and Scholarly Ambivalence
In modern historical research, beginning with the works of Gershom Scholem and Isaiah Tishby, sharp criticism has arisen regarding the degree of Sasportas's consistency at the beginning of the affair [cite: 26]. These scholars pointed out that some of the original epistles that Sasportas sent in real time, which survived in various manuscripts, were far more moderate and hesitant than the sharp and resolute version he later printed in his book [cite: 1, 26].
This discovery led to two opposing interpretations in the history of research:
The interpretation of rewriting and self-aggrandizement: some argue that Sasportas suffered from a certain ambivalence toward Sabbateanism in its first months [cite: 1, 27]. In retrospect, after Shabbetai Tzvi's fraud had become clear and he had converted to Islam, Sasportas sought to rewrite his personal history, re-edited his epistles in a more extreme form, and concealed documents attesting to his hesitations in order to appear as a brave and lone fighter from the first moment [cite: 26, 27].
The interpretation of fear and reasonable caution: on the other hand, other scholars argue that Sasportas was compelled to word his early letters with caution and diplomacy because of the real physical danger that threatened the opponents of Sabbateanism in those days [cite: 1, 27]. The opponents of the movement suffered severe persecution, excommunications and physical violence within the communities, and therefore the fear of expressing a resolute position in public was justified [cite: 1]. Only later, when the storm had subsided, could Sasportas courageously reveal his true inner position and formulate it in all its sharpness [cite: 1, 27].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Literary Work and Its Historical Influence
The literary legacy of Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas is broad and varied, and reflects his different fields of activity as a rabbinic judge, halakhic decisor, kabbalist and teacher of Torah [cite: 1, 3, 6]. His various works display an exceptional level of scholarship and combine deep Talmudic knowledge with a capacity for systematic organization and cataloguing [cite: 4, 7, 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary and Historiographical Assessment
The work and Torah teaching of Rabbi Yaakov Sasportas constitute a dramatic milestone in the shaping of Orthodox thought and Sephardic scholarship in recent centuries [cite: 2, 15]. Sasportas was not merely a stringent halakhic decisor or a routine communal gatekeeper; he was the religious intellectual who set the value of doubt and reasoned criticism against the destructive messianic certainty of his time [cite: 2, 15, 29]. Through his struggle against Sabbateanism, Sasportas showed that true Torah authority does not draw on visions, revelations or personal charisma, but on absolute subordination to Talmudic law and to the tradition of ruling of earlier generations [cite: 12, 20, 29].
Jewish historiography through the generations has taken up the figure of Sasportas and given it opposing and fascinating interpretations: whereas modern scholars such as Gershom Scholem at times tended to see him as a rigid and overly strict figure, representing an uncompromising "attribute of judgment" that seeks to stifle creative spiritual forces, in the Torah and Hasidic world Sasportas was perceived as a spiritual hero who saved the Jewish nation from spiritual annihilation and from a mass entry into an anarchic movement of heresy [cite: 12, 26].
This distinctive reading reached its peak in the teaching of the Satmar Rebbe, Rabbi Yoel Teitelbaum, who saw in Sasportas a kindred spirit and twin soul [cite: 12, 29]. The Satmar Rebbe projected Sasportas's work onto modern reality, and saw his own struggle against Zionism as a direct continuation of Sasportas's war against Sabbateanism [cite: 12, 29]. In his eyes, Sasportas proved that the power of Torah truth is not measured by the number of those who believe in it, and that even when the masses of the House of Israel and their rabbis follow a passing messianic "golden calf," the duty of the true leader is to stand isolated, armed with pure halakha and the teaching of Maimonides, and to sound the alarm at the gate against the impending spiritual destruction [cite: 12, 29]. The legacy of Hakham Yaakov Sasportas thus remains an eternal testimony to the power of the individual who dares to raise a voice of reason, justice and halakha against the spiritual storms of his time [cite: 2, 15, 22].
